Fill your TFSA in January or contribute every payday? It depends on where the money comes from

Separate money you already have from money you are still earning. Compare a January TFSA deposit with monthly staging, test which half-year returns favour each, and price the cost of saving paycheques for a once-a-year deposit.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare a January TFSA contribution with spreading the same room across the year

$7,000 of TFSA room is used each year. The fund returns 6% a year and money waiting in savings earns 2%, taxed at 30% when held outside the TFSA and tax-free inside it. Returns are smooth and hypothetical; real fund returns vary month to month and can be negative for long periods. Fees are assumed to be inside the fund return. The TFSA dollar limits are CRA figures; available room also depends on past contributions and withdrawals.

The central idea

New TFSA room arrives on 1 January. If the money is already in your savings, depositing it in January and then deciding how fast to invest it inside the account usually beats keeping it outside, and investing it at once is ahead on average when the fund is expected to earn more than savings, though not in every year. If the money comes from paycheques, there is no lump sum to front-load: investing each payday puts it to work sooner than saving up for a January deposit.

01

One decision that is really two

Every January brings new TFSA room, CAD 7,000 for 2024, 2025 and 2026. A common question is whether to put the whole amount in at the start of the year or to contribute a little every payday. The answer depends on a question that is easy to skip: does the money already exist?

  • Money you already have, such as savings, a bonus or a maturing GIC, can be invested on 1 January or staged over the year. That is a choice between a lump sum and dollar-cost averaging.
  • Money you are still earning arrives with each paycheque. There is nothing to front-load. The only choice is whether to invest each instalment when it arrives or to let it build up in savings for a later deposit.

Mixing the two leads to the wrong comparison. Someone saving from a paycheque who reads that “lump sums usually beat dollar-cost averaging” may decide to save all year and deposit in January, which is the reverse of what that finding implies. This guide takes each case in turn and keeps a third question separate: whether the money waiting to be invested sits inside or outside the TFSA.

02

How TFSA room arrives

The first chart shows CRA’s TFSA dollar limits. The limit was CAD 5,000 from 2009 to 2012, CAD 10,000 in 2015, CAD 6,500 in 2023 and CAD 7,000 from 2024 to 2026; a resident who was 18 or older in 2009 and never contributed would have CAD 109,000 of room in 2026. CRA’s TFSA guide explains that unused room carries forward, that withdrawals are added back at the start of the following year, and that excess contributions are taxed at 1% a month.

Two consequences matter here. First, the year’s room is fully available on 1 January, so a single January deposit and twelve monthly deposits use the same room. Second, money deposited in January does not have to be invested in a fund that day. It can sit as cash or a savings product inside the TFSA, where its interest is not taxed, while you move it into the fund on your own schedule. The pace of investing and the account the cash waits in are separate decisions.

03

Money you already have: January versus staging

The default case uses CAD 7,000 already in savings, a fund return of 6% a year and a savings rate of 2%. The Bank of Canada’s policy rate was 2.25% on 23 October 2026; savings rates vary by product and change with that rate. The second chart follows the money through one year:

  • Deposited and invested on 1 January: CAD 7,420 by 31 December.
  • Deposited in January, moved into the fund one twelfth a month: CAD 7,290. The waiting cash earns tax-free interest inside the TFSA.
  • Invested one twelfth a month, the rest waiting outside the TFSA with its interest taxed at 30%: CAD 7,271.

On these smooth assumptions investing at once is ahead by about CAD 130, because on average half the money spends half the year in cash instead of the fund. FINRA’s page on dollar-cost averaging notes that it often produces lower returns than lump-sum investing, especially over longer periods, in exchange for lower risk of buying just before a decline.

The third chart shows the risk side. It keeps the default savings rate and changes the fund’s return in each half of the year. If the fund falls 20% from January to June and rises 20% from July to December, staging ends about CAD 937 ahead, because the later instalments bought at lower prices. If the fund rises 20% and then falls 20%, investing in January ends about CAD 458 ahead. In flat years the higher-yielding choice depends on the savings rate. Which cell a coming year will land in is not known in advance; the phased-investing guide follows the same choice over longer staging periods.

04

Money you are still earning: invest on arrival

For most people saving from employment income the money arrives in pieces. The fourth chart compares investing CAD 7,000 a year in twelve monthly instalments as each paycheque arrives with saving the same instalments in a taxable savings account and depositing them in one amount each 1 January.

Each instalment in the second path waits 6.5 months on average before it reaches the fund. After one year, the payday path is worth CAD 7,225, while the saved instalments, deposited on the next 1 January, amount to CAD 7,053. Repeated for 20 years, with CAD 140,000 contributed in both cases, the payday path ends at about CAD 265,793 and the January path at about CAD 259,448, a gap of about CAD 6,346.

There is no expected-return argument for waiting here: investing a paycheque when it arrives is the lump-sum choice for that paycheque. It also removes the temptation to spend the savings or to start guessing about the market, which the waiting-for-a-dip guide tests. If per-trade fees apply, weekly or very small purchases can cost more than they gain; the batched-purchases guide prices that tradeoff.

05

When the smooth answer is not the right one

  • The money may be needed soon. Savings meant for an emergency fund or a purchase within a few years should not go into a fund at all, whatever the TFSA calendar. The short-term goal guide shows the risk.
  • A crash early in the year would make you stop. Staging a lump sum over several months is a reasonable way to reduce regret if a large fall right after investing would lead you to sell. The expected cost in the default case is about CAD 130 on CAD 7,000; that may be a price worth paying for staying invested.
  • Withdrawals and re-contributions. Money withdrawn from a TFSA cannot be put back in the same year unless unused room remains. The re-contribution calendar explains the timing.
  • RRSP and FHSA questions differ. An RRSP deposit also creates a deduction, and the RRSP deadline falls 60 days after year-end. The RRSP and TFSA comparison covers that wrapper choice.

The TFSA shelters income and gains from tax; it does not reduce the fund’s risk. A balanced fund in a TFSA can still fall, and a loss inside a TFSA does not give back room, as the TFSA loss guide shows.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The first chart shows CRA’s published TFSA dollar limits for 2009 to 2026, reviewed 27 October 2026. All other charts use hypothetical editable inputs: fund returns and savings rates are teaching assumptions, not forecasts or the record of any fund. The Bank of Canada’s policy rate of 2.25% on 23 October 2026 is cited only as background for the default savings rate. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Canada Revenue Agency · MP, DB, RRSP, DPSP, ALDA, TFSA limits, YMPE and the YAMPE ↗

    Page dated 1 December 2025; reviewed 27 October 2026. TFSA dollar limits: CAD 5,000 for 2009–2012, 5,500 for 2013–2014, 10,000 for 2015, 5,500 for 2016–2018, 6,000 for 2019–2022, 6,500 for 2023 and 7,000 for 2024–2026. No 2027 limit was listed. The CAD 109,000 total is computed on this page.

  2. Canada Revenue Agency · RC4466, Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA), Guide for Individuals ↗

    Reviewed 27 October 2026 (the page is marked as cancelled, so newer CRA pages may supersede it) for carryforward of unused room, withdrawals added back at the start of the following year, the 1% monthly tax on excess amounts and the general tax-free treatment of TFSA income.

  3. FINRA · Dollar-cost averaging ↗

    Page dated 19 May 2026; reviewed 27 October 2026 for its description of investing equal amounts at regular intervals and its statement that the approach often produces lower returns than lump-sum investing, especially over longer periods.

  4. Bank of Canada · Target for the overnight rate (Valet series V39079) ↗

    Retrieved 27 October 2026: 2.25% on 23 October 2026, unchanged since June 2026 in the retrieved range. Background only; the 2% default savings rate is a hypothetical input.
